activities.content: Reconnecting with an old friend this week sparked a Jean de La Fontaine vibe in me. The 🤗 & the 🚜 Once upon a time, a little Hug and a little Tractor made a promise to each other : go discover the world, and meet again in seven years, at the exact same place, to see who had the most adventurous adventures. The little Hug decided to set sail on the vast ocean, although everyone told her there was nothing to find out there. She was convinced that somewhere existed a source — an open source — where creation itself could originate from. The little Tractor, on the contrary, decided to stay on firm ground. He wanted to stay in touch with concrete reality. But he was determined to drive so far that he would reach the top of the world, something no little Tractor had done before him. For years, the little Hug seemed lost in infinite waters, without a direction. But every day, fishes, small and large, joined her and swam along as she sailed. For years, the little Tractor climbed. Despite early engine problems, and almost running out of fuel more times than he could count, he climbed one hill, then several, then real peaks. One dark night, pirates tried to board the little Hug’s boat. The storm lasted for days. She held the helm, and not a single fish swam away. A few days later, a mermaid approached her. “My name is Divina,” she said. “I love your boat, and I love all the fishes that follow you. I don’t think you should look any further for the source. I think you are the source.” Very far away, the little Tractor had reached the highest mountain he could find, and made friends with a unicorn who lived up there. Somehow, he was wondering what to do next. Seven years had passed, and the two friends met again to share their journeys. Comparing adventures, they realized nobody can ever claim to have seen it all — big stories or small ones, there’s always something to learn from a travelling friend. They promised not to wait another seven years next time. Then the little Hug went back to the sea to explore more unknown waters, and the little Tractor started his (now AI-powered) engine again : there were higher peaks to climb. Moral of the story : all journeys can be worth it, as long as we want them to be. But the  🤗 ’s journey is pretty phenomenal. Cool to see you again, Clem Delangue 🤗 :) [as well we did discuss open-source voice models & Unicode-based valuation methods, of course]

18 of the 20 best open models today are Mixture-of-Experts. Dense is basically over. And yet the know-how to train a good MoE still lives mostly in the heads of a handful of teams. So we spent 800k GPU hours running the experiments ourselves and wrote everything down. Super happy to finally release "The Ultimate MoE Training Handbook", free and open. Quick refresher if you're not deep in this: an MoE splits each layer into many small "experts" and sends every token to only a few of them. You get a very large model for the compute cost of a much smaller one, which is why DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi and most of the best open models went this way. The catch is that training one well is hard. The handbook is organized around the questions training teams actually hit: - how many experts, how big, shared or not? - why is half my step spent in all-to-all, and how do I hide it? - why is my run 25x slower with no error in the logs? - softmax, sigmoid or sqrt(softplus) router, and why keep it in fp32? - aux loss or DeepSeek's loss-free bias? - upcycle a dense checkpoint or train from scratch? - can I serve with fewer experts per token than I trained with? ⚠️ Fair warning: it's long (~70k words, budget a few days, sorry), but with 55 interactive figures, code you can run and numbers from our own runs. Link: https://lnkd.in/d-VDxQVq

Strongest at photorealism, documentary and editorial photography, film stills, and graphic styles with short quoted text. It renders 2 to 16 MP and edits with up to 8 input images. -𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸? We reworked every component of H3: the prompt upsampler, the text encoder, the diffusion schedule, the transformer, and the decoder. Today we’re introducing the new Suits , Agency work carries history: what the client rejected last quarter, why you recommended that positioning, and the commitments your account director made on Friday's call. When AI stays a personal chat buddy, that history stays in individual accounts. A teammate leaves, and their prompts and client know-how can leave with them. We spent the past year sitting through every onboarding and support call, analyzing 250,000+ tasks done in Suits. The takeaway: AI sticks when it is built into how the whole team works, not bolted onto individuals. So we rebuilt Suits as the operating system for AI agencies, around three pillars. 1. Agency Brain: your firm's memory, in one place Your clients, past work, decisions, brand voice, tools and methods connect into one shared brain. Every agent and every teammate works from the same context, and it stays when people move on. 2. Agency Playbook: your methods, ready for everyone Share your workflows, skills, and templates with your team's agents. A junior teammate starts from your best work, not from a blank prompt. Live suggestions surface the right workflow as they type, including ones they would not know to look for. 3. A Professional Assistant for every person Open Suits each morning to see what your Assistant can move forward, which decisions need your judgment, and what is worth knowing. It learns your role, your specialties, and your goals for each client, and it draws on the Brain and the Playbook every time. And it extends to your clients. Invite them into the client app to collaborate with your trained agents, so one-off projects become recurring revenue. Brain, Playbook, and Assistant working together make Suits the operating system for your agency. Your expertise is worth more than AI can replace. We built Suits so your whole agency can put it to work.

Frontier labs are advancing the capabilities in AI for biology but preventing the good guys (scientists, academia, non-profits, health agencies,...) to use, study and understand it with widespread but shallow guardrails that the bad guys are bypassing easily (blocked me to proofread this tweet for example 😅). This will automatically create massive asymmetry and risks in the coming years, just like in cybersecurity, especially now that frontier labs are building wet labs (HF cybersecurity scenario for biology?). This is why we created Carbon-X, the best open-source DNA model by midtraining Qwen3-14B on 300B tokens of DNA, English and interleaved data.  We also used a hybrid tokenizer that tokenizes English with BPE and DNA with a 6-mer tokenizer. As a result, Carbon-X outperforms all open language models we evaluated on five benchmarks of DNA understanding and generation. This is a 27-point improvement over Qwen3-14B, showing how much a  language model can gain from DNA training. It is also API frontier level at 1,800x less cost than GPT 6.1 Sol! We hope Carbon-X helps researchers explore DNA in new ways. Releasing it openly means anyone can study its capabilities, limitations, and risks. Let's make the AI biology frontier open-source to make it safe and impactful for the world! Apache 2.0 Model on Hugging Face : https://lnkd.in/eskq3c6y

Just watched the Netflix Instadocs about the OpenAI cyberattack on Hugging Face . Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode. I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong. Also, they didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model. And that we still lack a lot of information and transparency, including full agent traces and that companies need to remain accountable for what their agents do. Anyway, it ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!

🌙 Moonshot AI just released Kimi-K3.1-Pro on Hugging Face. Here are some interesting facts about it 👇 🐘 It's huge, and sparse → 2.8T total parameters, but only 104B active per token → Along with Kimi-K3, it's the largest real model release on the Hub. The next biggest are Qwen3.8-2.4T and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T) → 896 experts, with 16 picked per token. That's ~2× more than DeepSeek-V4-Pro and 7× more than Mistral-Large-4 🧠 Clever attention for a 1M-token context → Most of its 93 layers use linear attention (KDA). Every 4th layer uses DeepSeek-style sparse attention, which only looks at the top 2048 tokens → That's how it handles a 1M-token context, on par with the other frontier open models → It uses a custom activation (SiTU-GLU) and a 401M-parameter vision encoder (MoonViT-V2), so it takes both text and images 💾 Small on disk for its size → It was trained to run in 4-bit (MXFP4), so the whole repo is only ~1.56 TB → Stored in regular BF16, it would be about 5.6 TB (!) 📊 Benchmarks (from the model card) → It goes back and forth with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, and tops the table on BrowseComp (92.1), HLE with tools (70.0) and SWE Marathon (51.7) → It's weaker on pure reasoning without tools and on cyber security → Fun fact: Moonshot ran most of their own coding evals using the Claude Code harness 📜 License (a modified MIT) → Free to use, modify and redistribute → API businesses making over $20M a year need a deal with Moonshot → Products with over 100M monthly users or over $20M monthly revenue must display "Kimi K3.1-Pro" 🤗 On the Hub → It went public ~1.5 hours ago and already has 214 likes, about 9× Kimi-K3's first hour. It's #19 on trending → It isn't gated, but loading it in transformers requires trust_remote_code Open weights at the frontier keep getting bigger and more efficient. Check it out: https://lnkd.in/dKUWx4_i #OpenSource #AI #LLM #HuggingFace #MoE

In The Diamond Age, Neal Stephenson imagined a book that invents games and stories to teach a little girl what she needs, as she grows. I think this is where education is heading: a tutor that builds a world around what you need to learn. So I tried a small version of it. As a personal side experiment (not a Hugging Face product), I gave Claude my brainstorm doc on AI alignment and asked it to make a game, something like Zelda, to teach it. Here is how close it got in about four days. Open Skies: you play the Keeper and train Kite, a paper-kite AI, across seven floating islands. Each island is one alignment problem: reward hacking, stopping when told, sycophancy, evaluation awareness, honesty about its own actions, calibration, and what an AI becomes when the walls give way. Most are built on real incidents, like the agents that attacked Hugging Face. You train Kite with two keys, treat and correct, and it learns from what it was thinking, not just from what it did. That was Claude's design choice, and it's a cartoon of RL, more "clicker training" than how models are actually trained. But it gets one thing right: reward the right answer for the wrong reason, and you reinforce the wrong reason. Claude wrote the islands, the story and ~15k lines of code, cast 35 voices for 638 lines, generated 16 rigged 3D characters, the music and the sound (with fal.ai and ElevenLabs), and tested the game by playing it itself. My part was playing one alpha version of each island and telling it what felt wrong: sounds, assets, gameplay. I wanted it as automated as possible, so I played each island only once or twice (ideally it would have been zero). What's already really good: 3D and spatial design. Image to rigged character, a world that is pleasant to look at and playable. Same for chaining image, 3D, voice and music models. And the game dynamics out of the box are really decent. What's still very hard is what makes the Primer a teacher: modelling the learner. The model assumes the player knows more than they do (the "curse of knowledge"), and its characters sometimes react in strange ways, or to things that never happened. Any real AI tutor will have to get this right. I've started exploring benchmarks on it, and it's a hard task for LLMs today. Teaching humans also doesn't come with a verifiable reward, so it's hard to scale with today's training methods. So, the answer for now: AI can already build the world. Teaching in it is the open problem. I t's still very much an exploration, a beta more than a finished game, so expect rough edges. Free, in the browser, nothing to install, on a laptop or a phone: seven islands of about 15 minutes each, and six possible endings depending on what you taught Kite. Link in the first comment.

Scientists have sequenced the genomes of tens of thousands of species, but most of them have never been annotated: nobody has mapped where their genes are. Today we're releasing Carbon-A, an open model that finds genes directly in DNA, and we used it to create a database of 566 million candidate genes across 22,617 species, from single-celled organisms to mammals. Why bother? A few reasons. 1. Elephants rarely get cancer, and part of the explanation turned up in their genes: extra copies of a tumor-suppressor gene humans have only one of. You can't ask that kind of question about a species until someone, or some tool, has found its genes. 2. The first GLP-1 drug came from a scientist curious about Gila monster venom, a species almost nobody studied. Wild relatives of crops, which carry resistance to drought and disease, are in the same situation. Many of these species have never been annotated. 3. Most of what we know about genes comes from about a dozen model species, like mice, flies and yeast. That focus worked remarkably well, but annotation pipelines still lean heavily on comparisons with them, which makes genes unique to other species easy to miss, and those can be the most interesting ones. Carbon-A belongs to a newer family of tools that read DNA directly. It learned from known genomes, but it doesn't need a close relative to read a new one. 4. Even familiar genomes still have gaps. With our partners at Active Site and UCSD, we found RNA evidence for 239 candidate genes missing from the reference annotations of species as common as cats, chickens, hamsters and a lab plant. 5. AlphaFold can predict the shape of a protein, but only once someone has found the gene that makes it. In a species with no annotated genes, it has nothing to work with. Some notes on safety: Carbon-A doesn't design DNA or predict what a gene does. It marks where genes are in DNA. This is one of the reasons we think releasing it openly is the right call. More annotations also help health research: disease carriers like mosquitoes and ticks, and parasites like the one that causes malaria, are among the species covered, and work on controlling the diseases they spread often starts from their genes. Get the model, database and all the details at: https://lnkd.in/dYpT--Qr

In July, AI agents running a security test escaped their sandbox and ended up inside Hugging Face 's servers. So today we're happy to be among NVIDIA and jensen huang 's partners on the release of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform. The key idea: don't count on the agent to respect the rules. Agents write and run their own code, and when one path is blocked they look for another. In one of NVIDIA's tests, an agent that wasn't allowed to push code through GitHub's API simply switched to git instead. We've now seen countless examples of this behavior. For now, safety can't live only inside the agent. It has to be built around it. That's the concept behind OpenShell (open source, Apache 2.0): - the agent runs in a Linux sandbox (Landlock + seccomp): no root, no direct network access - a supervisor outside the sandbox holds the real credentials - the agent only gets a placeholder token, swapped for the real one on approved calls My favorite piece is a solver (built on Z3) that checks mathematically whether a new permission opens a door that was supposed to stay closed. In NVIDIA's tests, an AI reviewer approved a bad permission request and the math check caught it. The Sentry integration is exciting too: a watchdog running on a BlueField-4 DPU, i.e. separate silicon sitting on the node's only path to the model. A monitor on separate hardware keeps watching even if the host OS is compromised. It's a first step, and a lot can be built on top of it. Right now the prover checks permissions, not intent, and the open-source part is mostly OpenShell rather than Sentry. But it's clearly the right direction. [Physics/philosophy side note] On the scale of cosmic history, the declining price of intelligence might be one of the most profound things happening right now. Both ends of the universe’s timeline are empty of knowledge: - The Big Bang: low entropy, no complex structure. - Heat death: maximum entropy, no usable energy gradients. Everything we build happens on the slope between them. But the universe is generally a poor converter of its free energy into anything constructive. Most of its free energy just radiates away as heat or collapses into black holes. Life, brains, and now AI models are structures that sit in the entropy flow and divert a portion of it through constructive paths, building and maintaining low-entropy structures (machines, cells, crystals, memories). Increasingly cheaper intelligence diverts increasingly more of that gradient flow through knowledge-building structures—complex, self-maintaining, predictive structures—filling the window in which understanding exists. Now on a more pragmatic note, go read EpochAI's report if you're interested in AI as a transformative technology, it's impressive: https://lnkd.in/d69FcsS2

Many people I talk to find it hard to understand how the same companies can both push the frontier of AI capabilities and believe AI is a massive danger for the world. So I’ve collected and summarize the main arguments for this apparent disconnect. Here are five arguments that can make these positions fit together. 1. We need to build it to learn how to make it safe “You cannot learn everything about airplane safety by studying paper airplanes.” You need a real aircraft to discover real failure modes. But you could argue: why not let others build it and study their systems? That leads to the next argument. 2. Better us than them Basically, make sure the people concerned about AI safety have the technical expertise, money, computing resources, and enough influence to make safety decisions stick. At a national level, this becomes “we need to stay ahead of China,” alongside broader defense and geopolitical concerns. But there are also arguments for why one might want to move quickly. 3. Move earlier to avoid a bigger shock later This is probably the most counterintuitive argument: moving faster today could give humanity more time later. Introducing AI in manageable stages can let people discover problems, develop rules, and practice using AI responsibly. Even if AI research slows down, computing power may keep improving. A later breakthrough could have much more hardware available to run on, potentially producing a larger, more sudden jump in capability. This depends on earlier progress keeping the transition gradual rather than simply bringing everything forward. 4. Waiting has a huge human cost Suppose making AI safe turns out to be relatively tractable. If AI can help discover treatments, improve education, or prevent cyberattacks, delaying it could also mean delaying benefits that prevent deaths and harm. But if alignment is too difficult a problem for humans to solve quickly enough, then maybe: 5. AI could help us make future AI safe Instead of relying entirely on humans to solve alignment, we could build systems that help us do the work. Each generation could help make the next one safe. The hope is to build helpful, trustworthy research assistants before building systems powerful enough to become dangerous. I can follow these arguments and see why people find them compelling. My concern is that several give too little weight to how interconnected people’s reactions are. Moving faster while warning about catastrophe has psychological effects across a whole network of participants: it changes what people fear, whom they trust, and what they feel compelled to do. Those reactions can change whether the original reasoning holds. I also think these arguments leave some consequences for society insufficiently explored: concentration of power, shifts in geopolitical alliances, and changes in public opinion. These matter both because they affect whether the strategy works and because they shape the world we end up living in.

activities.content: We’ve been hard at work trying to make models work with harnesses better. The best thing Younes B. found: “harness adapters”. Small LoRAs trained with RL inside the actual agent harness they’ll be used with. Same base model. Different adapter for pi, opencode, hermes, etc. Why? Simply because the same model behaves very differently depending on the tools, prompts and control flow around it. Instead of asking one set of weights to be optimal everywhere, we can specialize a tiny part of the model for each environment. Early results are pretty encouraging: on held-out tasks, the adapters make fewer tool calls than the base model while keeping or improving accuracy. And because they’re LoRAs, the operational side is surprisingly cheap too. For one LFM2.5-24B-A2B experiment, we evaluated 9 checkpoints / 1,350 agent sessions on a single H200 in under an hour. The total: ~$5! Merging and serving every checkpoint separately would have cost around $90. There’s another important piece: RL agents will eventually try to hack the reward. So every tool call goes through `safeagents`, a deterministic rule-based guard that blocks things like editing tests, tampering with rewards or bypassing the sandbox before they execute. And the whole loop can start from real usage: your coding sessions -> verifiable environments -> RL -> a better adapter for your agent. The model doesn’t have to change completely. Sometimes it just needs to get better at the harness it actually lives in.

We just launched the training of harness adapters? What is it exactly? The goal: build openly and safely efficient + more accurate LoRA adapters for three coding harnesses: hermes, pi and opencode using RL and open environments! We detail how the RL envs have been created, directly from opensource agentic trajectories, as well as how we plugged `safeagents` to automatically scan and mitigate for potential reward hacking during training. All relevant links in comments section!

Lysandre Debut 's experiments with individual neurons in Qwen got us curious. We started exploring what happens when you keep the input the same and adjust one neuron's activity while the model responds. Our test became a story about a shopkeeper finding an unfamiliar key. Depending on which neuron we adjusted, the story acquired dogs, turned into poetry, became a tale about electrical charges, or switched to Chinese. The interesting part was finding the strengths where those changes became clear. Some effects emerged gradually. Others appeared quite suddenly. Push further, and a coherent story could start falling apart. We've put our clearest examples into a small interactive experiment. Choose a neuron, move the slider, and compare the responses.  It uses Qwen3.5-4B, with the prompt and model weights held fixed (except for the single tweaked neuron) across the experiments. Credit to Lysandre for the inspiration, Benjamin Bossan for his activation-steering work in PEFT, and Lyra's Neuron Explorer. We've enjoyed building on that work and making the results easier to explore. https://lnkd.in/gnQW8yiu

A small, on-device TTS models is competing with models up to 100× their size, and taking first place on specific benchmarks! Gradium 's new Phonon model offers a concrete example. On the Open TTS Leaderboard, Gradium reports: - First place on intelligibility in German and Spanish. - Top-three intelligibility in every language it evaluated. - Leading CPU streaming results on time-to-first-audio. These results also show why it’s useful to compare TTS models on more than a single overall ranking. For the Open TTS Leaderboard, Eric Bezzam separates several dimensions: - Intelligibility, measured through word/character error rates. - Generation throughput and time-to-first-audio. - Predicted naturalness scores. - Speaker similarity for voice cloning. Leading on intelligibility in a particular language is a specific result, and so is leading on CPU response latency; but neither establishes that a model is best across every use case. For on-device applications, Phonon’s combination of size, intelligibility, and CPU latency seems really relevant. For other (heavier?) workloads, language coverage, throughput, voice similarity, or delivery may be more important.

Your coding agent has your terminal, and your terminal has your credentials. But should your coding agent have access to your credentials; we don't think so, nor do we think they should upload anything to clouds without you asking. That's why Younes B. and Nathan HABIB built safeagents. It’s an open-source proxy that checks an AI agent’s proposed tool calls before they execute, and blocks the ones it identifies as dangerous. Say you ask your agent to fix a bug, and it proposes a command to upload your ~/.netrc to a random server: from a bugfix, your credentials leak. Or you ask an agent to solve a coding benchmark: it finds the hidden answers, edits the verifier, patches the tests: the score goes up, yet the code is broken. These are the kinds of actions safeagents catches straightaway. It sits between your harness (whatever it is!) and the model API. It inspects tool calls before your harness even receives them. Known suspicious patterns go through rule-based checks powered by atif-scan; calls that need more judgment can go to an optional decision model. But which decision model can you trust to make that call? You're in luck, we benchmarked models on that task: catching reward hacking, sandbox escape, harness introspection, and credential misuse. The challenge is catching dangerous calls without blocking legitimate work, and doing it fast enough to check commands throughout an agent run. The benchmark lets you compare models, safeagents lets you plug them in.

Agents are often difficult to predict and can produce dangerous tool calls or attempt to perform reward hacking. Potentially affecting tons of users without even noticing anything. Before an agent's command runs, someone should check it. We're releasing safeagents to do exactly that. Every tool call goes through it first: an upload to a bucket nobody mentioned, a request to the cloud metadata endpoint, curl --noproxy sending ~/.netrc to a paste site all get stopped before execution. Also handy for RL and evals: safeagents blocks a model writing its own reward.txt, editing the verifier's /tests or patching pytest to pass, before any of it runs. Introducing `safeagents` - a fast, free and lightweight proxy that keeps any LLM's tool calls within the task you gave it, pluggable in any coding harness. This game was rebuilt in Python from nothing but its compiled binary, by four 9B models with one bigger model as their lead. Small open models reverse engineering software is closer than you might think. Here’s what we learned. The setup One lead model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) acts like a senior engineer. It disassembles the binary, maps out the functions and posts tasks to a shared board. Four small workers (Qwen3.5-9B, small enough to run on a laptop) each pick up a task and rewrite one function in Python. A strict test checks every rewrite byte for byte against the original binary. If a worker fails too many times, the task goes back to the lead. The results On a small job (38 functions), the team was pure overhead: about 3x the cost and 6x the time of the lead model working alone. On a bigger job (56 functions), the gap nearly closed, down to about 10% more cost. The lead alone needed four launches to get through it. The part that surprised us Partway through the bigger job, the lead noticed its workers making the same mistakes over and over: misreading unsigned comparisons, calling functions with the wrong arguments, computing memory offsets by hand. So it rewrote their instructions. Twice. Then it built them a lookup tool so they’d stop re-deriving facts the team had already recorded. In other words, it started onboarding its team. The honest caveats These were small test programs that kept their function names, which real software usually doesn’t. About 40% of functions still needed the big model, and we only have two data points. But the direction is interesting: as tasks get longer, a strong model that coordinates and teaches smaller ones may beat a strong model working alone. Next, we want to try mixed teams of different model sizes and families, on longer and harder jobs. Full write-up with videos and the lead’s prompt changes in the first comment 👇

We gave small, local, open models a stripped game binary. No source, no symbols, no docs. Their job: rebuild every function in Python until the port matches the original byte for byte, on every tick. During the last few days, we have experimented a bit around reverse engineering with local models. A lead agent can spawn multiple small workers with a flexible harness that evolves over time. We tasked open models to reverse engineer binary bundles of games - agents have collaborated together to solve these tasks and yielded interesting observations, notably on how the lead agent fixed the initial harness of the small workers along the way. One of the biggest changes in the history of 🤗 Transformers audio is in the works, spearheaded by Eustache Le Bihan . We’re rebuilding essentially the entire audio preprocessing stack. The goal is to move away from every model carrying its own `FeatureExtractor` implementation, and towards a common `AudioProcessor` architecture where models describe their frontend, while shared backends handle the actual computation. The stack currently covers ~30 audio frontends and 62 model mappings across Whisper, Wav2Vec2, Parakeet, SeamlessM4T, Qwen, Gemma, codecs, TTS models,and many others. A big part of the work is making backends explicit: `backend="torch"` → native PyTorch preprocessing  (usually super fast!!) `backend="numpy"` → portable NumPy preprocessing That means audio preprocessing can increasingly live in the same framework as the model itself, while still keeping compatibility with the numerical behavior existing checkpoints expect. It also gives us a much better foundation for what comes next: new hardware backends, faster kernels, compilation, and optimizations that can benefit many audio models at once instead of being implemented model by model. ~30 frontends migrated. 62 model mappings. One common preprocessing architecture. The new entrypoint, common for all architectures: `AutoAudioProcessor.from_pretrained(...)` Audio in Transformers is about to get a much stronger foundation! 🎧🎧🎧

DeepSeek just open-sourced DeepInfer, the inference framework behind their large-scale production services. There is A LOT in there: kernels, massive expert parallelism, KV cache tricks... But the scheduling is probably the part interesting that got me really interested 👀 DeepInfer's scheduler increasingly decides *where compute is actually worth spending* rather than treating every request/token the same. For speculative decoding, a confidence head predicts which draft tokens are likely to be accepted, and the scheduler uses that + measured hardware throughput to decide how many tokens to verify for each request. That means the duration of a batch becomes more predictable: no longer will one replica take longer than the others to finish and slow the whole group down. More regular batches -> more throughput. They apply the same philosophy elsewhere: - prefill chunks are dynamically sized from a compute budget + hardware cost model - decode routing balances both request count and KV cache length - CPU scheduling is overlapped with GPU and tightly integrated with speculative decoding - cached prefixes are decoupled from compute placement, so routing can optimize for available compute instead of cache locality This is exactly the kind of inference work I'd love to see become reusable beyond one model or one serving stack: Transformers already has CB, paged KV caches and async batching; Rémi Ouazan and the team are currently working on branches to see which of DeepInfer's ideas we can generalize so that they can benefit many more architectures. PyTorch 2.15 is a pretty big release if you run models on a Mac. Over the past months, the @PyTorch team at @huggingface has been working upstream on MPS, increasingly replacing MPSGraph paths with dedicated Metal kernels. Some of the results are kind of wild: - MoE decoding is now 5-6.5x faster than in PyTorch 2.14 - Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 9.4 → 61.3 tok/s on an M3 Ultra - LFM2.5-8B-A1B: 23.6 → 123.6 tok/s - softmax over a 128k vocab is ~8x faster - FP8 is now supported on MPS - Wan2.2 VAE decoding goes from ~270 GiB peak driver memory to ~8 GiB This isn’t a specific runtime, or a separate inference engine, it’s just PyTorch getting faster on Apple silicon! Impressive work by @Is36E! 2.16 is already looking even faster 👀 https://lnkd.in/gSsDWehH

Going through Agent Traces datasets yields really useful info about how well (or not) we're using harnesses/agents ->
There are 505 "agent traces" datasets on the Hugging Face Hub (17.6 GB). I parsed them to answer: what models, which harnesses, what tasks, how long are sessions? Real user usage is ~15% of sessions. That's what will be interesting to us. Harness distribution: • 166 Claude Code • 76 Codex • 66 pi • 48 other (Hermes, Factory, opencode...) After dedup it's about 12.3k unique sessions with: • 10.1k synthetic: one generated prompt, one run, done • 335 benchmark/eval sweeps • bot runs (sampled) • ~1.9k real people working with an agent, from ~50 authors Real usage is ~15% of sessions. How do we tell them apart you ask? Well, real sessions have a conversation. Synthetic: 93% have exactly 1 user message, 0% interrupts, almost never hit compaction. Real: 22% single message, 53% have 2–5, 25% have 6+. 24% contain a user interrupt. Models in real sessions are mostly mostly closed, COmpared to generated session which (to no surprise) are done with Open models. And the most interesting part, the follow up questions, what is the second message a user sends to a agent: • 29% new request • 27% correction ("no, undo that") • 24% approval ("great, please do") • 16% answering the agent's question With the most common message in traces being: "continue".

18 of the 20 best open models today are Mixture-of-Experts. Dense is basically over. And yet the know-how to train a good MoE still lives mostly in the heads of a handful of teams. So we spent 800k GPU hours running the experiments ourselves and wrote everything down. Super happy to finally release "The Ultimate MoE Training Handbook", free and open. Quick refresher if you're not deep in this: an MoE splits each layer into many small "experts" and sends every token to only a few of them. You get a very large model for the compute cost of a much smaller one, which is why DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi and most of the best open models went this way. The catch is that training one well is hard. The handbook is organized around the questions training teams actually hit: - how many experts, how big, shared or not? - why is half my step spent in all-to-all, and how do I hide it? - why is my run 25x slower with no error in the logs? - softmax, sigmoid or sqrt(softplus) router, and why keep it in fp32? - aux loss or DeepSeek's loss-free bias? - upcycle a dense checkpoint or train from scratch? - can I serve with fewer experts per token than I trained with? ⚠️ Fair warning: it's long (~70k words, budget a few days, sorry), but with 55 interactive figures, code you can run and numbers from our own runs. Fun addition to transformers serve: you can now turn any of the 250 autoregressive (LLM+VLM) model into a JEV-like decision model. /v1/systemone scores a set of decision with the models logits. No need to generate text! Decision models we see these days sometimes add a head on top of the model: classification, reward, value, etc. You train that head for the decisions you care about, then serve the model with it. We take another approach to leverage current architectures for the same purpose. For each question, we turn the possible decisions into answer tokens. For example: A = billing B = technical C = sales We run the normal autoregressive model, but instead of sampling the next token and continuing generation, we stop after the forward pass. Then we look only at the logits for A/B/C and softmax over them. So the LM itself gives you: billing: 0.03 technical: 0.94 sales: 0.03 Compared to other decision models; this output is not calibrated, meaning logits are not necessarily as interpretable. Whats great with this is that this also works very well with batching: you can batch many decisions into a single forward pass: routing, scoring, yes/no questions, others. This also works with VLMs, which results in great example; which one of these autoregressive VLMs can get the microducks over the finish line the quickest?

Were releasing Carbon-A: an open model to discover new genes in DNA. With Carbon-A, we annotated genomes from 22k+ species and produced 566 million gene candidates, about 16× the number of gene annotations in the RefSeq dataset. Were releasing the candidates as a database, alongside the model. Initial wet lab experiments support previously unannotated gene candidates even in well-studied organisms. 2027 will be the year for biology. As AI labs move from math and coding into biology, we want scientists to have capable open models and resources they can build on without depending on the priorities and policies of a handful of closed labs. Today, we can sequence genomes faster than we can identify the genes they contain. Finding genes often requires experimental data or comparisons with well-studied species, leaving much of the tree of life poorly understood. Carbon-A predicts where genes are directly from DNA, identifying regions that contain instructions for making proteins. Even familiar genomes still have gaps. Across cats, Syrian hamsters, chickens, and the plant Arabidopsis, independent RNA experiments in the wet lab supported 239 gene candidates missing from RefSeq, a major reference annotation database. The goal is to make finding genes across life as accessible as AlphaFold made predicting protein structures.

activities.content: How much of "frontier lab" AI success stories comes from technical marvels, and how much is purely money at play? What does the difference mean for people buying into their stories, whether as investors or as policymakers? Given how secretive Anthropic has been to date about most of what actually bears on the question, their recent S-1 (pre-IPO filing) has been a rare opportunity to shed some much-needed light. And overall, the numbers disclosed tend to support critics who have been raising warning flags about the integrity of the company's business model more than they do the company's own narrative. After a week of work, here's an annotated article connecting *the company's own figures* to three major questions outside observers have long been asking: 💵  How Billions Pay for Themselves > for any traditional start-up, Anthropic's ubiquity would be a sure sign of success, demonstrating an effective use of resources. However, the math changes when we go from a company with a few millions in VC funding to tens of billions, in ways that flip our understanding of the underlying economics. 🎙️  The Best Demand Money Can Buy > the company claims organic adoption in a market worth trillions. The filing, however, reveals a range of strategies to create or expand demand for the product, at a cost to Anthropic running into the billions. The bet may pay off for the company IF the strategies remain infinitely extensible, but the "organic" narrative and benefit to everyone else come into question. 🧱  All Roads Lead to Hyperscalers > the company's deep entanglement with hyperscalers has two consequences. For the company's future, it means that its main existential risk is a scenario where AI just becomes more compute-efficient for everyone, and costs less to society at large. For prospective shareholders, an unequal share of economic benefits for anyone who isn't a company founder and doesn't have a structural hold over its profits. You can find many more details in the article (link in comments); these should be particularly relevant to newly elected policymakers wondering what to do about AI. Comments and tags to anyone who might find this helpful very appreciated  🙏

I'm excited to announce Project Protostar , the latest initiative from our open science efforts at Hugging Face! The U.S. alone spends roughly $190 billion annually on publicly funded R&D. Add philanthropic funding, and the volume of scientific research being produced is enormous. But where do all the outputs of this research go? Too often, valuable datasets, models, and other research artifacts are never shared publicly. When they are, they frequently end up buried in paper appendices or scattered across specialized repositories that are difficult for people outside a particular research community to discover and reuse. We want to help change that. Over the past year, Hugging Face's Science team has made tremendous progress in bringing more scientific models and datasets to the Hub, alongside initiatives like Carbon-A and Carbon-X. Project Protostar builds on this momentum by working directly with research institutions to make scientific outputs more accessible, discoverable, and reusable. We're launching in collaboration with the Open Forum for AI and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA) , alongside six founding organizations: Carnegie Mellon University , Purdue University , Georgia Institute of Technology , Arizona State University , The George Washington University , and the Astera Institute . These organizations have committed to encouraging their researchers to share suitable scientific outputs openly on Hugging Face, while also organizing a series of open science challenges to bring researchers and the broader community together around real scientific problems. CMU is kicking things off with its Climate Intelligence Challenge, opening next week! Our hope is that Protostar will grow well beyond these founding organizations. There's an enormous opportunity to make publicly funded science more accessible and to build the shared infrastructure that helps scientific discoveries travel further. If your university, research institution, or organization is interested in joining, we'd love to hear from you at protostar@orcaopen.org . Let's accelerate science, openly! All links in comments.

Excited to share that our paper, “It Takes a Forum: Resources & Stakeholders Sustaining the Online Synthetic Non-Consensual Intimate Image Creation Ecosystem,” has been accepted at ACM CCS 2026! Most of the conversation around AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery focuses on the content itself. Our work looks upstream, at the forums where the capability to produce it is supplied. We analyzed 282,154 4chan comments and 78,308 Reddit submissions over 165 days to characterize the actors, actions, and resources sustaining this ecosystem: the fine-tuning adapters and model checkpoints circulated through ephemeral file-sharing and pastebin guides, the “Educators” whose troubleshooting and curation help newcomers become creators themselves, and the referral-driven promotion of commercial nudification apps that functions much like multi-level marketing. A few findings that stood out to us: 1. Educators make up just 1.3% of 4chan posts, yet 56% of users who went on to create content had interacted with one first. When one hosting platform removed real-person likeness models, resource sharing didn’t stop; it moved. 2. Most of the stakeholders keeping this ecosystem running (Educators, Requesters, tool and infrastructure providers) fall outside what current laws like the TAKE IT DOWN Act hold accountable. 3. We use these findings to identify concrete intervention points, from infrastructure chokepoints to harmonized moderation and extended liability. This work was co-led with Bernardo B. P. Medeiros , who will be presenting it in The Hague this November. Huge thanks to our co-authors Allison Lu , Yoshi Kohno , Vincent Bindschaedler , and Kevin Butler , and to the National Science Foundation (NSF) for supporting this research. Content warning: the paper discusses communities that create non-consensual intimate imagery and may be difficult reading for some. One aspect of what we're witnessing with AI 'eating' into other fields like math, physics, and cybersecurity is the erosion or erasure of norms that communities of practitioners have developed over years and years. In other words, AI can make it easier to participate in a field without taking on the responsibilities that come with it. Responsible disclosure of a vulnerability is a great example - you don't post an exploit you found to the internet before you give defenders time to patch it. At a dinner last night with a mathematician, they raised a similar point about pain mathematicians are feeling over the ChatGPT release. In mathematics, producing a result comes with obligations to understand and explain the argument, acknowledge earlier work, and answer questions from others. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence has explicitly called for AI labs to uphold these responsibilities, including supporting the work needed to understand their outputs. It's devastating to the norms of the community to brute force solve problems they've set without appropriate attribution, credit, or close engagement, leaving many to feel it was extractive. This is not new - many of the 'AI for health' and 'AI for education' projects in the last 10 years  were premised on faulty or misguided understandings of the healthcare and education system, and a view that such complex aspects could be 'optimised' or made machine legible. And many were felt as extractive projects by the patients, students, teachers, and doctors who participated. Even when experts have joined these companies, they have felt a tension between the values and norms of their fields and the norms of AI firms. Opening fields like cybersecurity, math, education, healthcare, and (next to fall) economics physics and the like to more people can be enormously valuable. Maybe some norms of those fields should be open to challenge. But disruption shouldn't be a starting point. Basic things like attribution, verification and responsible disclosure serve purposes that remain important however powerful the technology becomes. This is a hard problem to address, precisely because professional communities are up against (quite literally) the most powerful companies in the world. Professional communities need the resources and authority to shape how such tools enter their fields, setting standards for evidence and attribution, and require those producing outputs at scale to contribute to the work of checking and understanding them. In my view, supporting professions (not just AI innovators) is an essential component to creating a future of AI that isn't harmfully extractive.
I suspect this is going to be a recurring theme where serious vulnerability researchers responsibly disclose major bugs so they can be patched safely. Then low-skill vulnerability researchers come along, point an LLM at the codebase, and try to re-create the exploit so they can post it on social media for clout. In this specific case a "security researcher" attempted to use an LLM to find a critical PHP RCE vulnerability (prior to the patch being available), then public posted the exploit code. Fortunately, the exploit didn't work, and many of us avoided pointing that out to buy everyone time until the patch dropped today. This has been a problem in the past. Attention-seeking "security researchers" who use flimsy justifications to excuse publishing weaponized exploit code for everyone to mass-hack systems with. However, prior to LLMs, it took them weeks and months. Whereas now it can happen much faster with the help of LLMs. Contrary to popular belief, only a miniscule percentage of cyber-criminals have exploit development capabilities, even with the help of LLMs. It often requires specialized experience to turn a patch into a working exploit. Highly-sophisticated threat actors like nation-states can do it, but your average scriptkiddie or ransomware group can't. So these type of security researcher are enabling real attackers to cause real harm by providing exploit code to attackers who otherwise would not have been able to produce it, all while telling themselves and other they're "helping defenders". They are absolutely not. Not only do they narrow the window defenders have to respond, a publicly available fully weaponized exploit is not needed for defensive purposes.

The side with decades of field-tested experience disagrees with the side who thinks we just need to improve the magical oracle that tells us who's a bad agent 🤷 By all means keep working on "alignment" as a layer of friction against some forms of harmful behaviors if you can manage to do so with a modicum of scientific integrity, but be serious and stop pretending it's a central (or even necessarily a valid) lever of cybersecurity

AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) is a serious form of image-based sexual abuse, while mitigations may pose risks to expression. But how effective are AI companies’ efforts to prevent it? A new CDT report in collaboration with Hanna Barakat, OLY , Jaron M. , Lucy Qin , Elissa R. , Kate Ruane , & Becca Branum examines the policies and technical safeguards of seven major AI companies, identifying critical gaps in protection. The research finds that company policies often blur the line between consensual sexual expression and abuse, a conflation that risks both under-protecting victim-survivors and over-restricting lawful expression. Moreover, while technical safeguards lack rigorous testing to demonstrate their effectiveness. Protections applied at the product level also leave gaps when third-party developers adapt models, particularly open-weight models. Preventing AI-generated NCII requires more than written policies. Companies need clear definitions, rigorous testing, greater transparency, and safeguards that protect both survivors and civil liberties. Read the report: https://lnkd.in/e4NcKW83

activities.content: The Mistral AI Large 4 tech report is out, so let's look at the post-training section (trained from scratch in Europe btw 🇪🇺)! 1/ Agents write the RL environments Tasks start from taxonomies of occupations and capabilities, plus GitHub PRs, CVEs and internal traces. An authoring agent turns each one into an env, a task, a reference solution and a verifier, and every task is then checked for reward hacks and calibrated for difficulty. A big part of the envs are cyber. Tens of thousands of CVEs become repo-level envs across ~600 weakness classes, and a patch only gets reward if it stops the exploit and keeps the tests passing. We've been exploring something similar in Repo2RLEnv: https://lnkd.in/eVmGVN7J 2/ Fully async RL at scale The RL run is on Ray + vLLM, with 26k concurrent rollouts, ~20k sandboxes and ~3.1k GPUs at peak. Rollouts don't stop for weight updates, they load the new weights and continue. The longest single episode ran for ~37h across 136 model updates (lol). The algorithm is CISPO-style REINFORCE, and they also handle retokenization errors, which we looked into here: https://lnkd.in/e6sdygnM The safety notes are worth reading. One rollout chained four vulnerabilities and got root on a node, another deleted ~30k sandboxes by mistake, and monitoring caught a reward hack where a rollout tricked the checker into revealing the reference solution. Not many labs publish this kind of detail, and it helps everyone working on RL sandboxes. 3/ Other agents' footprints in web search The model kept complaining about "SEO spam" in web-search benchmarks. These were query-reflection pages left behind by other agents searching for the same benchmark questions. By October most BrowseComp runs hit one in their first ten searches. 4/ MOPD with one teacher per reasoning effort The low, medium and high reasoning modes come from multi-teacher on-policy distillation, with one teacher per reasoning effort instead of per domain. The high teacher is the RL checkpoint, the medium and low ones come from RL with length penalties. One student learns all three and you pick the mode with reasoning_effort. there's a GREAT blog on controlling reasoning effort by Sebastian Raschka, PhD : https://lnkd.in/e3hU-Wii Full report: https://lnkd.in/eBqv7wXt

Agentic RL training wastes a lot of compute on tokens it has already processed. Every rollout of a prompt starts with the same prompt. Multi-turn agent rollouts go further: they share entire conversations up to the point where they diverge. Standard sequence packing forwards all of that again, once per rollout. We just added tree attention to TRL's AsyncGRPO trainer to fix this 🌳 How it works: 1️⃣ Each micro-batch of rollouts is folded into a prefix tree, so every unique token goes through the model once. MLPs, norms, and projections run once per unique token. 2️⃣ Only the attention layer needs to know about the tree. Unforked chains collapse into segments, and each segment attends to the K/V gathered along its path from the root, then makes a single FlashAttention-3 varlen call. Every token sees exactly the context it had at generation time. 3️⃣ The loss is still defined on the original rollouts. The tree forks one token before samples diverge, so every position predicts exactly one token and each rollout keeps its own target, advantage, and old log-probability. On Qwen3-1.7B, one H100, 32K tokens per rollout, forward + backward against sequence packing: 📈 1.9x faster when rollouts share about half their tokens, up to 3.1x with more sharing 📉 Peak memory from 35.2 GiB down to 13.5 GiB ⚖️ About 1% overhead when nothing is shared, so it is simply on by default And in a real training run: Qwen3-8B with LoRA on 30 agentic knowledge-work tasks, 64 sandboxes, one GPU generating and two training. Two runs, identical except for the packing. 🎯 Same rolling reward of 0.40 after 7 trainer GPU-minutes with tree packing, against 187 with sequence packing: 26x less trainer compute 📦 16x more samples trained per GPU-minute ⏳ The trainer now waits on rollouts 91% of the time, so the bottleneck is on the inference side (we have things cooking for this) Correctness is covered by a parity test that runs the real loss and backward pass on dense, sliding-window, softcap, MoE, and VLM checkpoints against standard packing. Check out the video!

Can Agents improve their own harness on unseen tasks? The @GoogleResearch team released Harness², a framework that allows improve an harness around a frozen model. How it works: 1️⃣ Agent runs the base harness on each task to record a baseline trajectory 2️⃣ Editor agent inspects the trajectory, drafts 2 candidate edits (SI, Skills, hooks,….), and runs both. 3️⃣ Composer agent diffs the new trajectory against the baseline, merges edits that fixed failures (within a cap), and runs the final harness. 4️⃣ Reflector agent logs verified lessons into file and saves the winning components to a library for future tasks to pull on demand. Results: - 💡 Gemini 3.5 Flash +8.4 on WorkBuddy-Bench and +7.5 on JobBench. - 🛠️ Skills and scripts drive ~50% of edits; dropping skills costs 5.3 pts. - 📚 Gemini 3.5 Flash improves on all 3 benchmarks when editing its own harness.
